questions.text: Why preserve actual frame timestamps when a video may be sampled at different frame rates?

options.A: Frame indices alone always specify elapsed seconds regardless of FPS.
options.B: Timestamps remove the need to encode spatial positions within frames.
options.C: Timestamps preserve elapsed-time information that frame indices alone omit.
options.D: Timestamps guarantee that every brief event appears in the sampled frames.

questions.explanation: The same frame-index gap can represent different elapsed times at different sampling rates. Actual timestamps retain that temporal information but cannot recover events omitted by sampling.

questions.text: Ignoring timestamp and text overhead, a 60-second video has a budget of 9720 visual tokens and costs 81 tokens per frame. What is the highest affordable FPS?
questions.explanation: fps_max = 9720 / (60 × 81) = 2 FPS, giving 120 frames and 9720 visual tokens.

questions.text: parse_tool_call first returns json.loads(raw) if parsing succeeds, without schema validation. What happens for raw=' {"tool": "mouse_click", "coords": "somewhere"} '?

options.A: It returns the dictionary even though coords is a string.
options.B: It returns PARSE_ERROR because coords must be a numeric pair.
options.C: It converts the string into validated screen coordinates.
options.D: It executes a mouse click using the supplied coordinate value.

questions.explanation: The JSON is syntactically valid, so json.loads returns a dictionary. This helper neither validates the tool schema or coordinates nor executes actions.
